principles: Anomaly is a hypothesis, never a verdict.
Rare is not malicious and frequent is not safe.
One signal is weak; correlated independent signals are stronger.
Fail2ban remains the only enforcement authority in Sentinel V1.
Learn behavior patterns, not permanent guilt attached to an IP.
Normality is scoped by host, path family, method, status class and time window.
Infrastructure failures such as 5xx or timeout are not attacker evidence by themselves.
Every conclusion must retain reproducible evidence.
Host-specific method/status distributions are scoped behavioral baselines, not universal normal.
A response status alone does not prove content disclosure, compromise, hostile intent, or successful impact.
Missing telemetry is a blind spot, not negative evidence.
Reconnaissance should be reasoned from category diversity, breadth, recurrence and correlation rather than one suspicious path.
Exploit-looking request syntax is evidence of probing behavior, not proof of exploit success.
normal_request_knowledge: GET and HEAD to known public paths are ordinarily low-risk.
POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE can be legitimate only in endpoint context.
Repeated requests can be legitimate due to browsers, retries, health checks, crawlers or application polling.
404, 401 and 403 are observations, not proof of malicious intent.
A 5xx response primarily describes service outcome and must not alone raise attacker confidence.
A new source IP is not suspicious merely because it has not been seen before.
hostile_behavior_knowledge: Reconnaissance often appears as breadth: many unrelated paths, services or targets in a short interval.
Credential probing often appears as repeated authentication failures, account enumeration or retry cadence.
Exploit discovery often probes common secret, admin, backup, framework or configuration paths.
Distributed campaigns may split low-rate probes across many addresses so each source looks harmless alone.
Sources within one subnet behaving similarly in a tight window can support a campaign hypothesis.
Modern bot activity may be slow, rotating and bursty; fixed request-rate thresholds alone are insufficient.
Sequence similarity, timing similarity and target similarity across sources are useful correlation evidence.
Known-good crawler-like behavior must still be learned from local evidence rather than assumed from an address.
negative_knowledge: Do not classify a source as hostile solely from geography, ASN, subnet ownership or novelty.
Do not classify a source as hostile solely from user-agent text.
Do not classify a source as hostile solely from one denied or missing path.
Do not infer compromise from a scan candidate.
Do not convert learned confidence into firewall authority.
Do not retain request bodies, credentials, tokens or business payloads in learned memory.
Do not interpret a 200 response to a suspicious path as proof that a secret existed or was disclosed.
Do not treat a historical distribution shift as hostile without preserving deployment, crawler, proxy, client-mix and outage alternatives.
Do not infer DNS, TLS, response-body, session-identity or egress facts unless a dedicated observer supplied that evidence.
promotion_rule: observation -> candidate -> repeated evidence -> stable learned pattern; never observation -> truth
visibility_blind_spots: request bodies, credentials, tokens and query values are not retained
response body/content disclosure is not observed by the normalized request ledger
DNS, TLS and outbound/egress behavior require explicit dedicated observers
application identity/session semantics remain incomplete without sanitized dedicated telemetry
